title: Deloitte’s Cyprus Office Helped Abramovich Firms Relocate Billions in Assets in Apparent Bid to Sidestep Tax and Transparency
content:
The Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte signed off on backdated paperwork for companies beneficially owned by Roman Abramovich, which helped the firms retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to try to get around tightening tax and transparency laws, leaked files show.

By piecing together years of email correspondence and financial records, reporters found that in the mid-2000s Deloitte Cyprus discussed and helped to execute the transfer of assets — including bank deposits, yachts, and luxury real estate — in the wake of increased taxes and transparency requirements on foreign-owned and private firms in Cyprus ahead of its accession to the European Union in 2004.

Deloitte Cyprus worked closely on the plans with MeritServus, a now-U.K.-sanctioned Cypriot corporate services provider that was a division of Deloitte Cyprus before it was spun out as an independent firm in 2005.

The two firms advised senior staff at Millhouse Capital U.K. Limited, a firm managing assets owned by Abramovich, and Millhouse LLC in Russia.

title: The Uzbek President’s Son-In-Law Secretly Acquired a UAE Passport While Serving as a Top Security Chief
content:
At the 2023 UN climate change conference in Dubai Otabek Umarov watched in the wings as his boss, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, met with his United Arab Emirates (UAE) counterpart.

Sporting a crisp navy suit and tie, Umarov at the time was the second most important official charged with protecting the Uzbek president. Perhaps more importantly, he was –– and remains –– married to Mirziyoyev’s youngest daughter, and is widely seen as an influential behind-the-scenes power broker.

But on that December day in Dubai, Umarov carried a potentially career-ending secret: seven months earlier, he had covertly obtained an Emirati passport requiring his sworn fealty to the state led by the man his father-in-law was talking to, President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.

Uzbek military law governing the security post Umarov occupied at the time prohibited his second citizenship, and would have served as possible grounds for discharge from active duty.

title: Instead of Helping Ukraine’s Poor, Ferrexpo’s Charitable Donations Flowed to Companies Associated With Its Then-CEO
content:
In 2017, the mining giant Ferrexpo announced it had donated more than two percent of its annual revenue to a charity based near the company’s vast iron ore mines in central Ukraine. 

This charitable spending significantly outstripped the average of its industry peers, the London Stock Exchange-listed firm highlighted in an annual report. 

Yet just one year later, questions set in. 

Auditors from Deloitte noted in Ferrexpo’s 2018 annual report that they had been unable to conclude whether the charity, named Blooming Land, had in fact spent $33.5 million of Ferrexpo’s donations on charitable ends.

Ferrexpo halted donations to the charity, which it said had been set up to “independently” coordinate the firm’s corporate social responsibility spending, and commissioned an investigation into the matter.

But the results were inconclusive: an investigating committee said only that the funds “could have been misappropriated,” and that it was unable to determine the fate of the firm’s donations.

title: Inside the Collapse of a Surrogacy Agency That Cost Surrogates and Hopeful Parents Their Dreams and Money
content:
The promise was a seamless journey towards building a family. 

Advertising services across Ukraine, Albania, Georgia, Cyprus, and Mexico, the commercial surrogacy agency World Center of Baby presented itself as a one-stop shop that would help match hopeful parents with surrogates and coordinate complex medical and legal processes. 

Some of the agency’s surrogacy packages were priced at more than $100,000.

But in February 2026, the agency sent an email to prospective parents announcing that it was declaring bankruptcy in the U.S., where its apparent main corporate entity was registered in Florida as World Center Group Corp.

The announcement triggered chaos. Online forums lit up with intended parents looking for help, saying they had been abandoned by the agency, sometimes in the midst of their surrogacy process. Reporters spoke with six couples and two single intended fathers who said they had incurred financial losses ranging into tens of thousands of dollars. For some, that spelled the end of their dream of becoming a parent.

Meanwhile, surrogates either in the midst of fertility treatments or already pregnant were left unpaid and unsupported.
snippet: The promise was a seamless journey towards building a family.
creator: Ambra Montanari, Beatrice Petrella, Mariia Horban (NGL.media), Kevin G. Hall (OCCRP), Xhesika Tollia (Shteg.org), Kelly Bloss (OCCRP)

title: A Kidney Transplant, Ignored Advice, and a President’s Surprise Pick to Run a $160 Billion Pacific Island Mine
content:
Almost 40 years after it descended into a devastating civil war, the autonomous region of Bougainville is on the cusp of achieving independence from Papua New Guinea. At its heart sits Panguna, a long-shuttered gold and copper mine worth an estimated $160 billion.

To relaunch the Panguna mine and generate the type of economic development that could support the impoverished region’s bid for full sovereignty, Bougainville’s majority state-owned mining company spent around 10 months on a public search for an international partner, speaking to some of the world’s largest and most experienced mining companies.

But last November, Bougainville President Ishmael Toroama made a shock announcement: he had signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to redevelop the mine with Lloyds Metals and Energy Ltd, a publicly-traded Indian company with no background in major copper and gold extraction.

title: From Tehran to Texas: How a Convicted Iranian Pyramid Scheme Ringleader Built a New Life in the U.S.
content:
Texas-based Iranian filmmaker Mazyar Mahan’s ‘Exile Echoes’ won awards across multiple film festivals in 2025, by far his most successful release to date. The film features Iranian women recounting tales of resistance and escape from repression by Iran’s morality police over sepia-tinted montages. 

But back in Iran, Mahan left hundreds of people facing heavy financial losses and upturned lives after they invested in a pyramid scheme he co-founded, according to an Iranian court verdict. 

“They claimed their work was in gold and securities and promised a 15 percent monthly profit,” said 58-year-old farmer Jamal Ganji, who said he was led to believe his money would be managed by a U.S. investment company named Palinure. 

“They didn’t pay us any profits,” Ganji recalled. “They just kept saying, ‘We’ll give you points. Go spend your points and recruit more people.’” 

It was then that he confronted the reality that his investment was unrecoverable.

OCCRP reporters used judicial records, property records, and leaked databases to trace Mahan’s path from Tehran to Texas after he left Iran and evaded a prison sentence for his role in one of Iran’s most notorious pyramid schemes.

title: Pentagon Fuel Subcontractor Owned by Alleged Front for U.S.-Blacklisted Brothers
content:
The U.S. government bought millions of dollars worth of fuel for its consulate in northern Iraq from a company whose local subcontractor on the deal was owned by a man described by a U.S. official as a front in a company for two blacklisted Lebanese brothers, documents show.

The findings, based on contracts, court documents, public records, and corporate filings, raise questions about the thoroughness of the U.S. government’s due diligence over the beneficiaries of a contract to supply fuel to a critical diplomatic post in a volatile country.

In August 2022, a U.S. Department of Defense agency awarded a $2.7 million contract to Swiss-based Rhomax International AG for the supply of fuel to the U.S. consulate in Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous region of Iraqi Kurdistan. 

According to documents filed with the U.S. government, Rhomax subcontracted storage and distribution of the fuel to Tavrons Ltd, an oil logistics company registered in Cyprus and owned and directed at the time by Lebanese national Ibrahim Zaouk.
